o: We must keep only those words whose letters all come from a single keyboard row, ignoring case. For each word we can determine which row its first letter belongs to, then verify every other letter matches that row. In Example 1, "Hello" has 'h' (row 2) and 'e' (row 1), so it fails; "Alaska" and "Dad" use only row-2 letters and pass; "Peace" mixes rows. Example 2's "omk" mixes rows 1 and 3, so the answer is empty. With at most 20 words of length 100, any per-character scan is trivially fast — no clever data structures are needed.
k: Map each letter to its row once (via sets or an array indexed by character), then check membership in O(1) per letter.
Lowercase the word first to handle case-insensitivity uniformly.
It suffices to compare every letter against the row of the word's first letter.

a.n: Approach 1: Row Sets with First-Letter Anchor
a.i: Build three sets of lowercase letters, one per keyboard row. Lowercase each word, find which set contains its first letter, and accept the word only if every letter lies in that same set. This directly mirrors the problem definition and runs in linear time over total characters.
s: For each word, create its lowercase version.
Pick the set containing the first lowercase letter as the anchor row.
If every letter of the word is in that set, append the original word to the result.
a.t: O(N) where N is the total number of characters across all words — each character is checked once against a hash set in O(1).
a.sp: O(1) extra space — the three row sets have constant size (26 letters max); output space excluded.

a.i: A single regular expression can match words made entirely from one row: ^(qwertyuiop|asdfghjkl|zxcvbnm)+$ applied case-insensitively. This is concise and idiomatic but relies on regex backtracking machinery; it is mainly a neat alternative rather than a performance win.
s: Compile the pattern ^([qwertyuiop]+|[asdfghjkl]+|[zxcvbnm]+)$ with case-insensitive flag.
Filter words by testing full-string match, keeping originals that match.
a.t: O(N) — each word is matched against the anchored pattern in time proportional to its length.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the compiled pattern and output.

w: In an interview, present Approach 1: it shows clear reasoning about hashing/membership checks and generalizes easily. Approach 2 is a nice concise mention but avoid leading with regex since interviewers often prefer explicit logic. Pitfalls: forgetting case-insensitivity (always lowercase before checking), returning the original-cased word rather than the lowercased one, and assuming non-empty words (guaranteed here, but guard lw[0] otherwise). Edge cases: single-letter words always pass; mixed-case words like "AlAsKa" still pass. Follow-ups might ask to handle arbitrary keyboard layouts (pass rows as input) or to return counts instead of words — both are direct adaptations of the same row-mapping idea.
